name: Florence Cathedral (the Duomo)
label: Duomo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazzale Michelangelo' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazzale Michelangelo' (way/233265213): middle (4 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/43768260: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Santa Maria del Fiore' (184 m across).

text.description:
Florence Cathedral, formally Santa Maria del Fiore, is the great marble church whose great dome rises above the city. Work began in 1296 and the dome, engineered by Filippo Brunelleschi, was finished in 1436. It is still the largest masonry dome ever built, and it went up without a temporary wooden frame to support it. The walls are faced in bands of white, green and pink marble, and the ornate west front is a 19th-century addition, completed in 1887. The cathedral stands with the Baptistery and Giotto's Campanile in Piazza del Duomo, part of the UNESCO-listed historic centre.

Up close the building is too big to fit into one frame. From the left side of the terrace you get a wide, raised view of the dome rising above the terracotta rooftops, with the river and its bridges in the same shot. The cathedral is the focus, but the city around it makes the picture. It is a free viewpoint and easy to reach, but it fills up fast at sunset, so arrive early and claim a spot at the railing. If you want a higher, clearer view, San Miniato al Monte is a steep walk uphill from the piazzale.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral stands in Piazza del Duomo in the historic centre of Florence. The viewpoint, Piazzale Michelangelo, is on the hill across the Arno to the south-east.
text.directions_text: For the cathedral itself, take tram T1 or T2 to Valfonda - Stazione Santa Maria Novella and walk south-east, about 11 minutes on foot. Alternatively, take tram T2 to San Marco Università and walk south, about 9 minutes on foot. For the viewpoint, Piazzale Michelangelo lies south-east of the cathedral across the Arno, about 21 minutes on foot in a straight line, with a climb at the end. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole scene, then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the dome closer. The cathedral is over a kilometre away, so it looks small at 1x. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a big sweep of sky and rooftops, because the dome will become very small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazzale Michelangelo (left side of the terrace). A wide, elevated panorama of the cathedral dome rising above the terracotta rooftops, with the Arno and the bridges in the same frame. At the left side of the terrace. The cathedral lies to the north-west, and from here you can see the dome above the rooftops, with the Arno and its bridges in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the dome on one of the upper intersections, with the river along the lower third. Keep the horizon level. Zoom in a little (2x-3x) so the dome stands out from the rooftops, but leave the river in view. If the terrace is crowded, wait for a gap or hold the phone slightly above the heads in front of you. San Miniato al Monte, on the higher hill, is a good alternative viewpoint with fewer obstructions.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the dome to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. At dusk, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the wall to keep the phone steady. Panorama mode works well for the full sweep of the skyline if you pan slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset. Arrive early at sunset, as the terrace fills quickly.

text.access_note: Piazzale Michelangelo is an open public square, but the cathedral is a working place of worship and entry to it and the dome may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From about 1.3 km away the dome appears small at the default lens (1x), so zooming helps.
Piazzale Michelangelo sits on a hill, so the last part of the walk from the city centre climbs.
Phone cameras tend to overexpose bright skies at sunset, so lowering exposure helps keep colour in the sky.
The cathedral is a place of worship, so entry to the interior may carry dress-code or ticket rules.

name: Uffizi
label: Uffizi
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazzale degli Uffizi' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazzale degli Uffizi' (way/23298781): middle (159 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/477279033: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Galleria degli Uffizi' (210 m across).
notes: Photographed from the courtyard between the two wings.

text.description:
The Uffizi is Florence's great Renaissance art museum, but for a phone photographer the real picture is outside, in the long courtyard in front of it. Two tall, matching wings run down either side of a narrow open square towards the River Arno. At the far end a Doric screen frames the view without blocking it, and the Ponte Vecchio shows in the distance between the arms of the colonnade.

Giorgio Vasari began the building in 1560 for Cosimo I de' Medici, as offices for the city's administration (uffizi means 'offices'). It was finished in 1581. Vasari stressed the perspective by giving both facades continuous roof cornices and unbroken cornices between the storeys, and by adding three long steps along the fronts. That is why the lines pull your eye so strongly towards the river. The niches between the columns were filled with sculptures of famous artists in the 19th century, which give you good detail shots.

The best viewpoint is at the north end of the courtyard, so walk to that end and face south towards the Arno. Keep yourself in the middle so both wings look symmetrical. The square gets very busy, so early morning before the museum opens, or after dark, gives you the clearest view. If you want a wider view of the river, with the Uffizi sitting alongside the Ponte Vecchio and the Palazzo Vecchio tower, Ponte alle Grazie is a good second choice.
text.geographic_location: The Uffizi is in the Historic Centre of Florence, right next to the Piazza della Signoria, with its courtyard opening onto the River Arno.
text.directions_text: The nearest tram stop is Valfonda - Stazione Santa Maria Novella (tram T1 and tram T2). The Uffizi lies to the south-east of it, about 17 minutes on foot. San Marco Università (tram T2) is also close, with the Uffizi to the south, again about 17 minutes on foot. Florence has no metro, so most people walk the last part. Once you are in the historic centre, head for the Piazza della Signoria and the Uffizi courtyard is right beside it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so both wings of the colonnade fit in and their lines run towards the river. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched version. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pull the Ponte Vecchio closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazzale degli Uffizi (north end of the courtyard, shooting south toward the Arno). The symmetrical colonnaded courtyard of the Uffizi, converging toward the Arno, with the Ponte Vecchio visible in the distance between the arms of the colonnade. Walk to the north end of the courtyard on Piazzale degli Uffizi and face south towards the Arno. From there the colonnaded courtyard runs away from you towards the river, with the Ponte Vecchio visible in the distance between the arms of the colonnade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the centre line on the middle of the courtyard so the two sides mirror each other. Hold the phone level, because tilting it makes the walls lean. For a different shot, take a close-up of the statues in the niches between the columns. If you want a wider view of the river, with the Uffizi, the Ponte Vecchio and the Palazzo Vecchio tower together, go to Ponte alle Grazie.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the far end of the courtyard to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the stone keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning before the museum opens, or at night, when the courtyard is quietest. At other times it is very busy with visitors.

text.access_note: The courtyard is an open public square, but going inside the Uffizi needs a museum ticket, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ponte Vecchio
label: Ponte Vecchio
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lungarno degli Archibusieri' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Lungarno degli Archibusieri nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5342094: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ponte Vecchio' (126 m across).

text.description:
The Ponte Vecchio is Florence's old stone bridge over the Arno, lined with small jewellers' shops and crossed on foot by a steady stream of visitors. The current bridge dates from about 1339-1345 and has three shallow arches, the middle one spanning 30 metres. It was the only Florence bridge spared in the Second World War. Above the shops runs the Vasari Corridor, built in 1565 to link the Palazzo Vecchio with the Palazzo Pitti.

Most people photograph the bridge from the crowded Ponte Santa Trinita. The riverside walk also gives close reflections in the water. The bridge's back shops, added in the seventeenth century, are visible from upriver, so look for those jutting out over the water.

Keep the arches and the water in one frame and let the bridge sit across the picture. If you want the classic profile with the hills behind, Ponte Santa Trinita is the alternative. For the wider view with the Duomo and Palazzo Vecchio, try Piazzale Michelangelo and use your phone's zoom.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Florence, where the Arno runs between the Uffizi side on the north bank and the Oltrarno on the south bank.
text.directions_text: From the tram stop Valfonda - Stazione Santa Maria Novella (tram T1 and tram T2), the bridge lies to the south, about 1 km away. Head south towards the river and the bridge, then follow the north bank of the Arno to Lungarno degli Archibusieri, at the far end of the street near the Ponte Vecchio. From the Duomo, walk south-west towards the river. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the three arches. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you stand close to the river wall and want to include the reflections. Telephoto (2x-5x) is useful for the shopfronts and the covered passage.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Lungarno degli Archibusieri (north bank, at the far end of the street near the Ponte Vecchio). The bridge's three arches seen from river level, with the covered passage on its side leading toward the Uffizi. On Lungarno degli Archibusieri, on the north bank at the far end of the street near the Ponte Vecchio. Face south-west and you see the bridge's three arches from river level, with the covered passage on its side leading toward the Uffizi.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the arches along the lower third, with their reflections in the water. Keep the horizon straight so the arches don't look tilted. For the bridge in profile with the hills behind, walk to Ponte Santa Trinita instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge's stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out. If the sun is low, try a Live Photo, which lets you pick the best frame of the moving water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is quieter. Sunset spots in Florence get crowded, so allow extra time if you go then.

text.access_note: The riverside street and the bridge are open to pedestrians, but the Vasari Corridor and the Uffizi terrace need a ticket and advance booking, so check the official site before you go.

name: Santa Maria Novella
label: Santa Maria Novella
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza di Santa Maria Novella' (5 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza di Santa Maria Novella' (way/95537273): point nearest the subject (123 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/449369047: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilica di Santa Maria Novella' (121 m across).
notes: 'santa maria novella' alone is mostly the railway station.

text.description:
Santa Maria Novella is a Dominican church and a World Heritage Site, and its front is one of the easiest buildings in Florence to photograph. The facade is covered in geometric patterns of white and green marble, which show up clearly even on a small phone screen. The lower part dates from the 14th century. The upper part, with its round window, its pediment and the big S-shaped scrolls at the corners, was designed by Leon Battista Alberti and finished in 1470. Building the church took almost 200 years, and it was consecrated in 1420.

The square in front is what makes the picture work. It is open, so the whole facade fits in the frame, with the two obelisks and the lawns as a foreground. Guides say you can photograph the facade from almost anywhere in the square, so you can take your time choosing a spot without queuing for it.

Look for the details too. In 1572 an armillary sphere and an astronomical quadrant were added to the blind arches at either end of the lower facade. They make a good close-up with the zoom. Take one wide shot of the whole front first, then move in on the frieze, the round window or the scrolls. If you want people in the foreground for scale, they are easy to find. If you want the square to yourself, go early.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Florence, on the square that carries its name, just south of the tram stops that serve Santa Maria Novella station.
text.directions_text: Take tram T1 or tram T2 to Valfonda - Stazione Santa Maria Novella; the basilica is to the south, about 3 minutes on foot. Alternatively, get off at Alamanni - Stazione Santa Maria Novella and walk south-east, about 4 minutes on foot. Once you reach the open square, turn to face the marble facade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the square, which fits most of the facade. If you are close and cannot fit it all in, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the round window, the frieze and the scrolls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza di Santa Maria Novella (anywhere across the open square, facing the facade). The green-and-white marble facade of the basilica filling the frame across the open square, with the two obelisks and lawns in the foreground. Anywhere across the open square, facing the facade. The facade fills the frame, with the two obelisks and the lawns in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the vertical edges of the facade up with them, so the building does not lean. Keep the phone level and at chest height, and leave a little lawn and obelisk at the bottom for depth. Then take a second shot with the zoom on the upper part of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the marble to focus. If the sky is bright, drag the exposure slider down slightly so the white stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames, as walkers will cross the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is quiet and the marble facade is well lit.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the basilica itself is a church and may be ticketed or restricted inside, so check the official site before you go; photography inside may be limited in some areas, so check the signs.
claims_not_in_sources: The square is open and public, so no ticket is needed to photograph the facade from outside.
Gridlines help keep the vertical edges of a building straight in a phone photo.
Interior photography rules and entry conditions may differ from the exterior, so visitors should check the signs and the official site.

name: Piazzale Michelangelo
label: Piazzale Michelangelo
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/233265215: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Michelangelo Square' (196 m across).
notes: The classic view over Florence: photographed from the spot itself.

text.description: Piazzale Michelangelo is a broad terrace on a hill in the Oltrarno district, just south of the historic centre, and it gives the classic view back over Florence. It was designed by Giuseppe Poggi and built in 1869, when Florence was the capital of Italy and parts of the city were being rebuilt. The tree-lined Viale dei Colli winds up the hill and ends here. The square is named after Michelangelo and has bronze copies of some of his marble works that stand elsewhere in the city: the David and the four figures from the Medici Chapel. Poggi's neoclassical loggia dominates the terrace. It was first planned as a museum of Michelangelo's work. The spot photographs well because the whole city lies spread out below you. The view takes in the heart of Florence from Forte Belvedere to Santa Croce, including the Arno and its bridges, the Ponte Vecchio, the Duomo, Palazzo Vecchio, the Bargello and the bell tower of the Badia Fiorentina. For a phone, start with a wide shot to show the whole sweep, then zoom in on one landmark, such as the Duomo or the Ponte Vecchio, for a second, tighter picture. Include a little of the terrace wall or a statue in the foreground to add depth. Take a few frames, as people often walk through the view.
text.geographic_location: In the Oltrarno district, on a hill just south of Florence's historic centre, across the Arno. It sits at the end of the tree-lined Viale dei Colli.
text.directions_text: From the Duomo, head south across the Arno into Oltrarno, then climb the hill; the square is on the hilltop. From Santa Maria Novella station, walk towards the Arno and Oltrarno and check your map app for the route up the hill. No tram stop is close, so you can also go by taxi or hired scooter. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole city view, then the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural frame. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Duomo, Palazzo Vecchio or the Ponte Vecchio.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The square itself is the subject, so you are standing in it. Walk to the terrace wall on the city-facing side for the view, and look around you for the statue copies and the loggia.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level. Put the Arno and its bridges on a lower third line and let the skyline fill the middle. Include part of the terrace wall or a bronze statue in the foreground for depth. Use panorama mode for the full sweep from Forte Belvedere to Santa Croce, and move the phone slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the Duomo to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. After sunset, try night mode and brace your elbows against the wall to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into early evening usually gives softer light and a good sky over the city. The square can be busy at popular times, so expect people in the frame.

text.access_note: A public hilltop square; check the official site before you go for any local restrictions or events.

The square is a public open space with no entry ticket.
Late afternoon and early evening usually give softer light.

name: Boboli Gardens
label: Boboli Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kaffeehaus' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kaffeehaus' (node/11119522358): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24267141: large area 'Boboli Gardens' (1114 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
The Boboli Gardens are a large park behind the Pitti Palace, laid out in the mid-16th century as the Medici family's private garden. They were made for Eleonora di Toledo, wife of Cosimo I de' Medici, and are still among the best-known early formal Italian gardens. They now cover about 11 acres. Inside you find wide gravel avenues, statues, big fountains, artificial grottoes and a stone amphitheatre cut into the hillside, with an Egyptian obelisk at its centre. The Fountain of Neptune, nicknamed the Fountain of the Pitchfork, stands on the slope above.

For photographs, the gardens give you two kinds of picture. Down in the garden, the long avenues, the amphitheatre and the tree-ringed pond with the Isolotto island make good layered scenes. Its terrace looks across the rooftops to the Duomo, with the dome near the centre of the frame. Guides name it as the garden's best panoramic spot. Trees partly cover the view, so it is less clean than some other Florence viewpoints, but it is a pleasant place to pause and shoot.

If the trees get in your way, the Giardino del Cavaliere is another viewpoint in the gardens, with a wide panorama toward the hills south of the city. Move a step or two sideways to find a gap in the branches. Rather than rushing, take several frames from slightly different spots.
text.geographic_location: The Boboli Gardens lie directly behind the Pitti Palace and rise on Boboli Hill.
text.directions_text: Florence has no metro, and no tram stop is close, so walk. From Santa Maria Novella station or the Duomo, walk to the Pitti Palace; the gardens are directly behind it. Once inside, walk up through the gardens and head for the pale green building on the far left, which is the Kaffeehaus. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the terrace view of the rooftops. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Duomo's dome. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) in the amphitheatre or along the avenues.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Kaffeehaus (terrace on one side of the pavilion, reached by walking in and heading for the pale green building on the far left). The Duomo and the city skyline seen across the rooftops, with the dome near the center of the frame. On one side of the pavilion. You reach it by walking in and heading for the pale green building on the far left.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the dome near the centre of the frame and use the rooftops as a foreground. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level. Shift a step sideways so branches do not cross the dome. Try one wide shot and one zoomed shot of the same view. If you want a different angle, the Giardino del Cavaliere offers a wide panorama toward the southern hills.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the dome to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Panorama mode can work well for the sweep of rooftops, but hold the phone steady and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Arrive early in the day, when it is easier to find clear sightlines through the trees.

text.access_note: Entry rules and any ticketing for the Boboli Gardens are not covered here, so check the official site before you go.

name: Piazza della Signoria and Palazzo Vecchio
label: Piazza della Signoria
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza della Signoria' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza della Signoria' (way/23298643): middle (163 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23298643: 'Statua equestre di Cosimo', the best-known feature inside 'Piazza della Signoria' (163 m across).
notes: Merged: the palace and the Loggia dei Lanzi stand on the square.

text.description: Piazza della Signoria is Florence's great open-air meeting place, and the Palazzo Vecchio is its centrepiece: a heavy, castle-like town hall with a crenellated front and a tall tower. The square works well for phone photos because everything you want is at ground level and close together. The palace is the backdrop, and the statues give you foreground. The replica of Michelangelo's David, over 5 metres high, stands at the palace entrance. The Fountain of Neptune, from 1575, is nearby. The Loggia dei Lanzi at the side is a row of wide arches that works as a sculpture gallery, with pieces such as Cellini's Perseus. The palace dates from the 14th century. It is still the city's town hall, and parts of it are open as museums. The square itself began taking shape from 1268. A round marble plaque in front of the fountain marks where Savonarola was executed in 1498. For the classic shot, stand in the middle of the square and face the palace front, with David and Neptune in the foreground. For a variation, shoot from the Loggia, where the sculptures frame the palace behind them. The square is busy for most of the day, so go early if you want clear views without crowds. Check for any building works nearby, as they have been a nuisance in recent years.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Florence, in front of the Palazzo Vecchio. The square is close to Piazza del Duomo and is the gateway to the Uffizi Gallery.
text.directions_text: Walk from the tram stop Valfonda - Stazione Santa Maria Novella (tram T1 and T2). The square is to the south-east, about 15 minutes on foot. From San Marco Università (tram T2) it is to the south, also about 15 minutes on foot. If you are already at the Duomo, the square is a short walk away. The square is pedestrian-only, so arrive on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole palace front, the tower and the statues in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view with less stretching at the edges. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower top, the battlements and individual statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza della Signoria (middle of the piazza, facing the palace front). Palazzo Vecchio's crenellated facade and tower across the open square, with the replica of Michelangelo's David and the Fountain of Neptune in the foreground. In Piazza della Signoria, in the middle of the square facing the palace front. From here you see Palazzo Vecchio's crenellated facade and tower across the open square, with the David replica and the Fountain of Neptune in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so the palace does not lean. Place David or the fountain low in the frame to add depth. For a different view, step into the Loggia dei Lanzi and use the arches and sculptures as a frame around the palace facade behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Keep the phone level, because tilting it upwards makes the tower lean inwards. Portrait mode can work on a single statue, but check that the edges look clean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is quieter.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, pedestrian-only, but entry to Palazzo Vecchio's museum areas may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Palazzo Pitti
label: Palazzo Pitti
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza de' Pitti' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza dei Pitti' (way/787858333): middle (226 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1637338: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palazzo Pitti' (280 m across).

text.description:
Palazzo Pitti is a huge, stern Renaissance palace on the south side of the Arno, a short walk from Ponte Vecchio. Its rough, heavy stonework and the long rows of arched windows, repeated three times across the front, give it a strong, almost aqueduct-like look. That rhythm is what makes it work so well in a photo.

The core of the building dates from 1458, when the banker Luca Pitti had it built as his town house. The Medici family bought it in 1549 and made it the main home of the ruling family of Tuscany. It was given to the Italian people in 1919 and is now the largest museum complex in Florence. The main block alone covers 32,000 square metres.

The best frame is from Piazza de' Pitti, the open square in front of the main facade. The whole symmetrical front sits neatly in the space, and you can line up the centre of the building with the middle of your screen. Early morning or an overcast day gives soft, even light on the stone, without harsh shadows between the windows. If you want a second view, the rear of the palace rises above the upper slope of the Boboli Gardens, with the garden in the foreground. The gardens are ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Palazzo Pitti is on the south side of the River Arno, a short distance from Ponte Vecchio. The Piazza de' Pitti is the open square directly in front of its main facade.
text.directions_text: There is no tram stop close by, so this is best done on foot. From the Duomo, walk south-west towards the river, cross the Arno and continue to the square in front of the palace. From Santa Maria Novella station, walk south-east towards the river, cross to the south bank and continue to Piazza de' Pitti. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

text.description: The Bargello is a severe, battlemented medieval palace in the middle of Florence, and its plain stone walls and tall tower make a strong, simple subject for a phone. Building began in 1255, and it is described as the oldest public building in the city. It was built first for the Capitano del Popolo and then, from 1261, for the podestà, the city's highest magistrate; later it served as police headquarters and a prison, and it has been a national museum since 1865. The two lower storeys are the oldest part. The third storey, built with smaller stones, was added after a fire in 1323, and you can see the change in the stonework if you zoom in. The museum inside is known for Renaissance sculpture, including works by Michelangelo and Donatello. The best-known interior photo subject is the courtyard with its well and staircase, but that is inside the museum, so these tips are about the outside. The best open-air view is from Piazza di San Firenze, where the crenellated facade and tower rise across the square and the Badia Fiorentina sits nearby in the frame. The square is more open than the surrounding streets, so you can step back and fit more in. Take a few frames: one wide shot with the tower and the neighbouring buildings, one closer shot of the battlements and stonework, and, if you like, one from Via del Proconsolo, where the side wall and tower recede along the street.
text.geographic_location: The Bargello is in the historic centre of Florence, near Piazza di San Firenze and the Badia Fiorentina, with its side wall running along Via del Proconsolo.
text.directions_text: Florence has no metro, so the easiest way in is on foot from a tram stop. From Valfonda - Stazione Santa Maria Novella (tram T1 or T2), head south-east; it is about 1 km on foot. From San Marco Università (tram T2), head south; it is about 800 m on foot. Once you are near, look for Piazza di San Firenze and the tower rising above the rooftops. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the facade and tower. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the whole tower in, or when shooting along Via del Proconsolo. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the battlements and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza di San Firenze (north-east corner of the square, facing the palace's facade and tower). The Bargello's crenellated medieval facade and tall tower rising across the square, with the Badia Fiorentina nearby in the frame. From there you face the palace's crenellated facade and tower, with the Badia Fiorentina close by in the frame. The Bargello is to the north-east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line, holding the phone upright so the walls do not lean inwards. Include a little of the square in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a second angle, walk to Via del Proconsolo, where the side wall and tower recede along the street between the old palaces.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. If you use ultra-wide, keep the phone level and stay away from the frame edges, where buildings can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime shows the stonework and battlements clearly. The palace also photographs well in the evening, so it is worth a second visit if you are nearby. Use night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The outside of the palace can be photographed from the public square and street, but the museum inside is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
The Galleria dell'Accademia is the museum that holds Michelangelo's David, which makes it one of the most popular stops in Florence. The statue has stood here since 1873. Before that it was outdoors on Piazza della Signoria. The museum itself is older: it was founded in 1784 by Pietro Leopoldo, Grand Duke of Tuscany. It is smaller than the Uffizi, but it drew about 1.46 million visitors in 2016, so expect company.

For a phone photographer the appeal is simple. David is a single, strong figure, and a phone picture of him works best when you keep the shot plain. Stand back, keep the whole figure in the frame and let the surroundings stay quiet. Nearby you can also photograph Michelangelo's unfinished Prisoners, which look rough and dramatic beside the finished statue. The paintings in the other rooms are mostly Florentine works from the 1300s to the 1500s.

Outside, a quick shot of the museum front gives you a record of the visit. Inside, there will be people in the way, so be patient and wait for a gap. Rules on photography and flash can change, so check the official site before you go. That is also the place to check how tickets and entry work.
text.geographic_location: The Galleria dell'Accademia is in central Florence, close to the San Marco Università stop on the tram T2 line and the university buildings.
text.directions_text: The nearest tram stop is San Marco Università on tram T2, about 1 minute on foot, with the museum to the south. From La Marmora Orto Botanico (also tram T2) it is about 6–7 minutes on foot, heading north-east. From the Duomo, walk to the San Marco Università tram stop area; the museum is next to it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) and stand well back so the whole statue fits. Use telephoto (2x or more) for a closer shot of the face or hands when people block the view. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only for the museum front outside, because it can stretch the statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Photograph the museum front from the pavement outside. Inside, use the spot where visitors are allowed to stand, as far back as the room lets you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and turn on the gridlines. Keep the statue in the centre, with the head and feet both inside the frame. Crouch slightly to lessen the upward angle, which keeps the proportions looking natural. Take one wide shot, then one close shot using telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if bright areas look washed out. Keep the flash off. Hold the phone steady with both hands and take a few shots so you can pick the sharpest. Night mode can blur if people move, so use it only if the room is very dim.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early or late in the opening hours is likely to be quieter, which gives you clearer views. Indoors the light is much the same all day, so choose your time for the crowds, not the sun.

text.description:
Fiesole is a small hill town about 5 km north-east of Florence, and it has looked down on the city for a very long time. It began as an Etruscan settlement, was taken over by the Romans, and later rivalled Florence before being conquered by it in 1125. Dante mentions its people in the Divine Comedy. From the fourteenth century wealthy Florentines built country villas here, and the town is still known for them and their gardens.

For a phone photographer the appeal is the mix of old stone, terracotta rooftops and wooded hillside, with Florence in the valley below. The Roman theatre is a good extra stop. It has 19 tiers of stone seats and is about 34 m across, and part of it has been restored so you can read its shape. Leonardo da Vinci is also recorded as testing early flying models on these hills.

Take a first wide shot from here, then walk on and look for gaps between buildings, stone walls and steps to use as foreground. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines, and tap the brightest part of the sky if the hillside looks too dark. Some sites in town may be ticketed or have visiting rules, so check the official site before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the rooftops to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. If you are shooting a view with a lot of detail, use a panorama and move slowly with the phone held level.

text.description:
Santa Croce is the principal Franciscan church of Florence and the largest Franciscan church in the world. Building began on 12 May 1294 and the church was consecrated in 1442. The pale neo-Gothic marble façade is much younger, dating from 1857 to 1863. Its architect, Niccolò Matas, worked a Star of David into the design. Inside are the tombs of Michelangelo, Galileo and Machiavelli, which is why the church is also called the Temple of the Italian Glories.

It photographs well because the façade sits at the end of a large square, so you can step back and fit the whole front into your phone frame. The Dante monument gives you a foreground, and the old palazzi on either side make a natural frame. For the full-façade view, go to the piazza in front of the basilica, near the Dante monument. If you want a second, wider view, Piazzale Michelangelo shows Santa Croce as one small part of the city skyline, so it suits context shots rather than a close picture of the church.

Plan your visit around the square's events: it hosts the Calcio Storico in June, which may affect access on those days. Take a wide shot first, then walk closer and use the zoom for details such as the marble patterns and the Star of David.

text.description: The Basilica of San Lorenzo is one of the largest churches in Florence and sits in the middle of the city's main market district. It is the burial place of the Medici family's leading members, and it claims to be among the oldest churches in the city, first consecrated in 393 AD. The building you see today was begun around 1419 to designs by Filippo Brunelleschi and is a milestone of Renaissance architecture. Its outside is the main photographic draw. In 1518 Michelangelo was asked to design a marble façade, but it was never built, so the front is still plain, rough brick. That bare surface makes a strong, simple shape in a photo, and the market stalls and cafés in the square add life around it. The bell tower dates from 1740. The best frame is the straight-on view of the front from the square, with the façade filling the picture and the market activity along the bottom edge. Guides suggest golden hour in the late afternoon, or early morning before the market crowds build up. If the square is busy, wait for gaps in the crowd rather than trying to edit people out later. For a different feel, try the street-level view along Via dell'Ariento, where the basilica sits at the far end of the market's bustle.

text.description: Ponte Santa Trinita is a graceful stone bridge over the Arno, and it photographs best as a whole, seen side-on from the riverbank. Three very flat, elliptical arches sit low over the water, and on a calm day the river gives you a softer second version of them as a reflection. The bridge carries statues of the four Seasons, so you can include a little sculpture as well as the arches. The bridge was built by Bartolomeo Ammannati between 1567 and 1569, after floods had destroyed earlier bridges on the same spot. It is described as the oldest elliptic arch bridge in the world. It was blown up in August 1944 and rebuilt in 1958 using original stones, and the missing head of the statue of Spring was found in the river bed in 1961. Ponte Vecchio is the next bridge upstream to the east, and Ponte alla Carraia is the next one downstream to the west. Stay on the embankment and keep your phone level so the arches don't lean. If you want a different angle, the riverside road at Lungarno Guicciardini shows the bridge with the statue of Spring in front and the Lungarno Corsini buildings beyond.

text.description:
The Baptistery of St John is the eight-sided building in the middle of Florence's cathedral square, faced in marble and set between the Duomo and the Archbishop's Palace. Most scholars place its origins in the 11th or 12th century, and Dante was baptised here. It photographs well because its shape is simple and clear, and the bronze doors give you detail shots as well as the wide view. The south doors were led by Andrea Pisano, and the north and east doors by Lorenzo Ghiberti. Michelangelo is said to have remarked that the east doors could stand at the gates of Paradise.

From here the Baptistery's façade, the Duomo and Giotto's Campanile can all fit in one frame. Cafés fill the square during the day, so an early-morning visit gives you a clearer shot. If the square is too busy, Piazza San Giovanni on the other side of the building is quieter and shows the exterior without the main cathedral crowds.

Leave a little space around the building in the frame. Then take a second, closer photo of the doors or the marble patterns. Keep the phone upright for the Campanile and Duomo together, and turn it sideways for the Baptistery on its own.

From San Marco Università (tram T2), walk south-west for about 9 minutes on foot (approximate). You will come out in the cathedral square, and the Baptistery is the eight-sided building in front of the Duomo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close and want the Baptistery, the Duomo and the Campanile in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the façade. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the door panels and marble detail from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza del Duomo (in front of the Baptistery's main façade, across the square from the cathedral). The octagonal Baptistery's marble façade with the Duomo and Giotto's Campanile in the same frame. The Baptistery is just to the west of you. From here the marble façade, the Duomo and Giotto's Campanile can all fit in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the phone level so the vertical edges of the building stay straight. Put the Baptistery on one side of the frame and let the Duomo and the Campanile fill the other side. For a calmer alternative, try Piazza San Giovanni on the other side of the building, which shows the exterior away from the main crowds.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Baptistery's marble to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail. If people walk through the frame, take a few shots in a row or try a Live Photo and choose the cleanest moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the cafés fill the square and the crowds arrive.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the open squares; entry to the interior may be ticketed or restricted, and restoration work may affect parts of it, so check the official site before you go.

name: San Miniato al Monte
label: San Miniato al Monte
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Scalinata dell'Abbazia di San Miniato al Monte' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Abbazia di San Miniato al Monte' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/184781037: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilica di San Miniato al Monte' (71 m across).

text.description: San Miniato al Monte is a Romanesque basilica standing on one of the highest points in Florence, and it is often described as one of the most scenic churches in Italy. The geometric green-and-white marble facade is the main subject for a phone photo. Its pattern is crisp and graphic, and it looks good from the foot of the staircase, where the old iron gates and lower arches frame it. The facade was probably begun around 1090, with the upper parts added in the 12th century or later. An eagle, the symbol of the cloth merchants' guild that looked after the church, crowns the top. The mosaic of Christ between the Virgin and St Minias on the facade repeats the subject of the larger mosaic inside the apse. Work on the present church began in 1013, and Olivetan monks, who run the adjoining monastery, still live here. For the best picture, stand on the central axis of the staircase and shoot the facade head-on. The dark ironwork against the pale stone makes a more distinctive image than a close-up of the stonework. Keep to one side of the steps so you do not block other visitors, and be considerate if a service is taking place. For a second picture, go up to the terrace and turn your back to the church. From there you can photograph the city below, with the Duomo, Palazzo Vecchio and the Arno.
text.geographic_location: San Miniato al Monte stands on a hilltop in Florence, south of the Arno and looking over the city. The basilica sits within its own walled complex of monastery and cemetery.
text.directions_text: From the Duomo, head south across the Arno and then climb uphill towards the basilica; the church is on the hilltop and is the big white-and-green building at the top. The climb is steady, so allow extra time. The staircase you want is the one leading up to the facade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the head-on facade shot. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you cannot fit the facade and the gates in from where you are standing. Use telephoto (2x or more) for the eagle and the mosaic.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Scalinata dell'Abbazia di San Miniato al Monte (central axis of the staircase, facing the facade). The white-and-green marble Romanesque facade straight on, framed by the historic iron gates and the lower arches. Face north towards the facade. From here you see the white-and-green marble front straight on, framed by the historic iron gates and the lower arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep your phone level, centred on the middle of the steps, and turn on the gridlines so the vertical lines of the facade stay straight. Let the dark ironwork form a frame at the edges. If you want a different view, the terrace in front of the church looks back over Florence with the Duomo, Palazzo Vecchio and the Arno, but you will need to turn around and leave the church behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale marble keeps its detail and does not turn white. Take a few shots in case people walk into the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light warms the pale marble.

text.access_note: The basilica is a place of worship and a working monastery, and the interior has limited visiting hours and is restricted during services, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: San Miniato al Monte is on the south side of the Arno, across the river from the Duomo.
The walk from the Duomo is uphill and takes some effort.
Keeping the phone level and using gridlines helps keep the facade's vertical lines straight.
Lowering the exposure slider can stop pale marble from overexposing.

name: Orsanmichele
label: Orsanmichele
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Via dei Calzaiuoli' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Via dei Calzaiuoli nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/442508011: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chiesa di Orsanmichele' (43 m across).

text.description: Orsanmichele stands on Via dei Calzaiuoli, the busy pedestrian street between Florence's cathedral and Piazza della Signoria. It looks like a tall, plain stone block, and that is partly because it began as something else. The first building here, finished in 1290, was an open loggia for the grain market. It was later closed in and turned into a church, and its name comes from an old 'orchard of Saint Michael' on the site. It photographs well because of the statues set into niches around the outside. They represent the patron saints of Florence's main guilds, and some are by Ghiberti, Donatello and Nanni di Banco. The statues you see on the street are replicas, and the originals are kept in the museum inside. Inside is also Orcagna's tabernacle, built between 1352 and 1359 and often called a high point of Italian Gothic sculpture. From there the building is a short way off to the west, and you can fit two niche statues and the tall Gothic wall above them into one upright frame. Standing across the street gives a wider angle than standing right beneath the walls, where you would have to point the phone steeply upwards. The street is a main walking route, so wait for gaps in the crowd and keep an eye on passers-by while you frame the shot.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Florence, on Via dei Calzaiuoli, roughly between the Duomo and Piazza della Signoria.
text.directions_text: From the tram stop Valfonda - Stazione Santa Maria Novella (tram T1 or T2), walk south-east for about 800 m (roughly 10 minutes on foot) to reach Via dei Calzaiuoli. From the Duomo, walk south along Via dei Calzaiuoli; from Piazza della Signoria, walk north along the same street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is too crowded to step back, and use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a close shot of a single statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Via dei Calzaiuoli (opposite pavement, looking west toward the building's northwest corner). Two exterior niche statues in their tabernacles, with the tall Gothic stone facade rising above them, framed in one vertical shot. From here the two outer niche statues in their tabernacles and the Gothic stone wall rising above them can all fit in one upright shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and turn on the gridlines. Line the edge of the building up with a vertical grid line, put the niche statues in the lower half and leave the tall wall above them. Try to keep the phone level, because tilting it upwards makes the walls lean inwards. If people are walking through, wait a moment for a clear gap.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright sky is washing out the stone. Take a few shots in a row, as people keep walking through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: A weekday morning is suggested as the quieter time on this busy pedestrian street.

text.access_note: The statues on the outside can be photographed from the public street; the museum and upper rooms inside have limited opening and the church is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting a phone upwards to photograph a tall building makes vertical lines lean inwards.
Ultra-wide (0.5x) helps when you cannot step back far enough because of crowds on a fairly narrow street.
The church is a place of worship, so modest dress may be expected inside.
The walk from the tram stop (about 800 m) takes roughly 10 minutes at a normal pace.

name: Forte di Belvedere
label: Forte di Belvedere
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazzale Michelangelo' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazzale Michelangelo' (way/233265213): middle (4 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24879633: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Forte di Belvedere' (248 m across).

text.description:
Forte di Belvedere is a large fortress on the hill south of the Arno, set above the Boboli Gardens. The architect Bernardo Buontalenti built it between 1590 and 1595 for Grand Duke Ferdinando I de' Medici, and it is the second and largest fortress in Florence. It was meant to protect the Medici, the Pitti Palace and the Oltrarno side of the city. A villa inside, the Palazzina di Belvedere, is older than the fort and was designed by Bartolomeo Ammannati around 1570. Galileo is also linked to the place, because he used the fort for astronomical observations.

On a phone, the best picture of the fort itself is from across the valley, from Piazzale Michelangelo. You see the pale walls and the villa on their wooded hilltop, with the green of the Boboli Gardens around them. From there the fort is a fairly small part of a very wide view. Use the telephoto lens to pick it out, and use the default lens (1x) for a wider shot that keeps the hillside and the roofs of the Oltrarno below it. If you walk over to the fort, the cobbled Costa San Giorgio, which leads down from it, with cypresses nearby, makes a good foreground. The gate and approach road on Via di Belvedere are also worth a look. Check the angle on the spot, as these are only suggestions. The fort is not always open to visitors, so check the official site before you go. You can still photograph the outer walls from outside.
text.geographic_location: The fort stands on a hill in the Oltrarno, the district south of the Arno. It sits above the Boboli Gardens and Pitti Palace, and west of Piazzale Michelangelo.
text.directions_text: From the Duomo, cross the Arno and head uphill into the Oltrarno towards Costa San Giorgio, which leads up to the fort. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the fort closer. Use the default lens (1x) when you want the whole hillside and the city around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazzale Michelangelo. The fort on its hilltop across the valley, seen from the famous terrace above the city. From the terrace you look across the valley at the fort on its hilltop, with the city spread out below you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the fort in the upper third of the frame and let the wooded slope and the rooftops fill the rest. Turn on the gridlines to keep the horizon level. If you also walk to Costa San Giorgio, use the cobbled lane and the cypresses as a foreground leading towards the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the fort's pale walls to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright. Zoomed-in shots shake more, so hold the phone with both hands and brace your elbows on the wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to suit the fort best, because the sun is behind you and lights the side of the fort facing the square. Late in the day you are shooting towards the sun, so expect a darker, more silhouetted fort.

text.access_note: Piazzale Michelangelo is an open public square, but the fort itself is not always open to visitors, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From Piazzale Michelangelo you look across the valley to the fort, which appears fairly small in the wider view, so zoom helps.
The fort is about 15 minutes on foot from Piazzale Michelangelo, heading west (915 m x 1.3 / 80 m per minute).
From the Duomo you cross the Arno and climb into the Oltrarno towards Costa San Giorgio.
Morning sun comes from the east, behind someone standing on Piazzale Michelangelo, so it lights the east-facing side of the fort; late-day sun would be in front of the camera.
Handheld zoomed shots are more prone to camera shake, so bracing the phone helps.

name: Giotto's Campanile
label: Giotto's Campanile
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza del Duomo' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza del Duomo' (relation/310421): middle (245 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/251650632: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Giotto's Campanile' (21 m across).

text.description: Giotto's Campanile is the slender bell tower standing beside Florence Cathedral, with the Baptistery close by. It photographs well because the walls are covered in patterned marble: white from Carrara, green from Prato and red from Siena. That gives a phone camera plenty of colour and texture even on a grey day. The tower is 84.7 metres tall and square, with sides of 14.45 metres. The first stone was laid on 19 July 1334, when Giotto was in charge of the works. He died in 1337, having finished only the lowest level, and the tower was completed in 1359. The spire he planned, which would have taken it to about 122 metres, was never built. Look at the lowest level for the rows of hexagonal relief panels. The ones you see are copies, as the originals are now in the cathedral museum. From the square you can fit the cathedral façade, the tower and the Baptistery into one picture. That is the classic view, and it is best early in the morning, before the square fills up. If you want a different angle, try the corner of Via dei Servi for a three-quarter view with the dome, or the entrance to Piazza San Giovanni.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Florence, on Piazza del Duomo, standing next to the cathedral and close to the Baptistery of St. John.
text.directions_text: Florence has no metro, and the centre is best covered on foot. From the tram stop San Marco Università (tram T2) it is about 590 m on foot, heading south-west. From Valfonda - Stazione Santa Maria Novella (tram T1 and tram T2) it is about 660 m on foot, heading south-east. Once you reach Piazza del Duomo, the tower is hard to miss beside the cathedral. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the façade, the tower and the Baptistery in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is crowded and you have to stand close. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the marble patterns and the relief panels.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza del Duomo. The cathedral's marble façade with Giotto's Campanile beside it and the Baptistery in the same frame. In the open part of the square facing the cathedral. From there the marble façade, Giotto's Campanile beside it and the Baptistery all fit into one picture. The entrance to Piazza San Giovanni, close by, shows how the tower, cathedral and dome sit together.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and hold the phone upright, not tilted back, so the tower's edges stay straight. Step back as far as the square allows, then use the default lens (1x) to take in the full height. For a different angle, the corner of Via dei Servi gives a three-quarter view with the dome, the Campanile and the cathedral together. Check it on the map before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright marble to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white stone keeps its detail. For a long row of buildings, panorama mode also works, if you keep the phone level and hold it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the square is quieter and the light is soft and golden.

text.access_note: The tower stands in a public square and you can photograph it freely from outside, but climbing it is a separate visit, so check the official site before you go.
